## Proof

We show the equality holds (assuming $X$ is integrable, so all conditional expectations below are well-defined).

**Notation.** Let $g(Y,Z) := E[X \mid Y, Z]$. The right-hand side is $E_{Z\mid Y}[\,g(Y,Z)\mid Y\,] := E[\,g(Y,Z)\mid Y\,]$, i.e. the conditional expectation of $g(Y,Z)$ given $Y$ (integrating out $Z$ conditional on $Y$). The left-hand side is $E[X\mid Y]$. So the claim is the **tower property** of conditional expectation:

$$E[X\mid Y] \;=\; E\big[\,E[X\mid Y,Z]\,\big|\,Y\,\big].$$

**Key fact.** $\sigma(Y)\subseteq\sigma(Y,Z)$, so conditioning on $Y$ is "coarser" than conditioning on $(Y,Z)$.

**Verification via the defining property.** Recall: $E[X\mid Y]$ is the a.s.-unique $\sigma(Y)$-measurable random variable $W$ satisfying
$$E[W\cdot h(Y)] \;=\; E[X\cdot h(Y)] \qquad\text{for every bounded measurable } h. \tag{$\ast$}$$

Set $W := E[\,g(Y,Z)\mid Y\,]$. By construction $W$ is $\sigma(Y)$-measurable. We check $(\ast)$ for this $W$.

For any bounded measurable $h$,
$$
E[W\cdot h(Y)]
\;=\; E\big[\,E[g(Y,Z)\mid Y]\cdot h(Y)\,\big].
$$
Since $h(Y)$ is $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, it can be pulled inside the conditional expectation (defining property of $E[g\mid Y]$):
$$
=\; E\big[\,g(Y,Z)\cdot h(Y)\,\big]. \tag{1}
$$
Now $h(Y)$ is also $\sigma(Y,Z)$-measurable (because $\sigma(Y)\subseteq\sigma(Y,Z)$). Applying the defining property of $g(Y,Z)=E[X\mid Y,Z]$ with the $\sigma(Y,Z)$-measurable test function $k(Y,Z):=h(Y)$:
$$
E\big[\,g(Y,Z)\cdot h(Y)\,\big] \;=\; E\big[\,X\cdot h(Y)\,\big]. \tag{2}
$$
Combining (1) and (2):
$$
E[W\cdot h(Y)] \;=\; E[X\cdot h(Y)]
$$
for every bounded measurable $h$. This is precisely condition $(\ast)$, so by a.s. uniqueness of conditional expectation,
$$
W \;=\; E[X\mid Y] \quad\text{a.s.}
$$

That is,
$$
E\big[\,E[X\mid Y,Z]\,\big|\,Y\,\big] \;=\; E[X\mid Y] \quad\text{a.s.},
$$
which in the problem's notation is
$$
E_{X\mid Y}[X\mid Y] \;=\; E_{Z\mid Y}\!\big[\,E_{X\mid Y,Z}[X\mid Y,Z]\,\big].
$$

**Conclusion.** The equality **holds** (almost surely), provided $X$ is integrable. This is exactly the law of iterated expectations (tower property), valid because $\sigma(Y)\subseteq\sigma(Y,Z)$ — conditioning on more information first and then averaging out the extra variable recovers conditioning on the coarser information.

### PROOF COMPLETE
